<description>
{
 "summary": "This change separates definitely unusable transaction outputs into a distinct container rather than keeping them in the primary in-memory TXO set. It also embeds key parent transaction metadata directly into WalletTXO objects so balance calculation and coin selection do not need to look up parent CWalletTx records. State transitions, wallet loading, and block disconnection routines are updated to maintain both sets and sync TXO states.",
 "problem": "After PR 27286 introduced in-memory tracking of all wallet TXOs, balance checking and coin selection iteration must traverse all historical outputs, even those spent long ago. For active wallets with substantial transaction histories, iterating through large numbers of confirmed-spent or conflicted outputs causes significant performance degradation.",
 "evidence": [
  "PR description: \"This TXO set is iterated for balance checking and coin selection preparation, which can still be slow for wallets that have had a lot of activity. This PR aims to improve the performance of such wallets by moving UTXOs that are definitely no longer spendable to a different map in the wallet so that far fewer TXOs need to be iterated...\"",
  "Follows up on merged PR #27286 ('wallet: Keep track of the wallet\\'s own transaction outputs in memory') and relates to PR #34360 which adds a 'WalletBalanceManySpent' benchmark for high-history wallet scenarios."
 ],

 },

<category name="wallet" title="Wallet">
## Covers

The bitcoind wallet: key and descriptor management, transaction creation
and coin selection, PSBT handling, wallet database (SQLite, and the
legacy BDB migration path), backup and recovery, rescanning, wallet RPCs,
and wallet-facing pieces of the GUI. Fee estimation is wallet when the
change is about how the wallet uses it.

Borderline: a descriptor or PSBT change that affects only `bitcoin-tx` or
RPC without wallet code is rpc, not wallet. An `interfaces::Wallet`
change is both wallet and ipc.

## What matters here

Fund safety first: anything that could lose keys, double-spend
unintentionally, create an unspendable output, or corrupt the wallet
database. Then backup, recovery, and migration correctness, including the
legacy-to-descriptor migration path that every remaining legacy user
must cross. Then privacy of transaction creation (address reuse, change
detection, fingerprinting). Then user-visible reliability: hangs, slow
rescans, confusing failures, wrong balances. Then features users have
asked for, with evidence they have asked.

The rubric does not ask whether Bitcoin Core should have a wallet. It
asks, given that it does, what a wallet user needs most.
